content:
Experimental evidence on accuracy comes from Bonilla López et al. (2018), who randomly assigned low-intermediate EFL writers (N = 139) to four feedback conditions and a self-correction control. A long-term advantage, measured four weeks after feedback provision, was evident only for direct corrections (Bonilla López et al., 2018). Notably, learners reported significantly lower cognitive load when revising after direct corrections on grammatical errors than after metalinguistic codes on grammatical and non-grammatical errors (Bonilla López et al., 2018). The authors acknowledge they could not employ an online physiological measure of cognitive load, so this self-report finding warrants caution (Bonilla López et al., 2018). The design is rigorous in its random assignment and delayed posttest, but the self-report measure limits what can be claimed about processing effort.

Learner preferences point in a different direction. In a survey of 70 students in a university ESL program in the southwestern United States, students favoured direct correction with metalinguistic explanations (215/447, 48.10%), followed by direct correction alone (111/447, 24.83%) (Liu and Wu, 2019). Their descriptive, non-randomised questionnaire design limits inference, and the authors themselves note the data are necessarily descriptive (Liu and Wu, 2019).

Evidence on revision behaviour is indirect. Zhang and Hyland (2018) observed a very limited range of revision operations in a second draft, with only seven of 35 errors corrected properly, and reported that automated feedback tended to highlight rather than correct errors. The study was a naturalistic case study of two Chinese students over a 16-week semester, so it cannot speak directly to coded feedback.

sentences: Research on written corrective feedback (WCF) in second-language (L2) writing increasingly treats metalinguistic codes—brief labels flagging an error without supplying the correct form—as a distinct feedback condition rather than a variant of direct correction.
This review surveys the project library's coverage of coded feedback, organised around three outcomes: writing accuracy, revision behaviour, and learner engagement.
The evidence base is narrow; only one source isolates codes experimentally.
The most direct evidence comes from Bonilla López et al. (2018), who randomly assigned 139 low-intermediate EFL writers to four feedback conditions and a self-correction control.
Their mixed-effect models showed that direct corrections and codes both enhanced learners' immediate grammatical and non-grammatical accuracy during revision (Bonilla López et al., 2018).
A long-term advantage, measured four weeks after feedback provision, was evident only for direct corrections (Bonilla López et al., 2018).
This is a rigorous design—random assignment, five groups, delayed posttest—and its central finding is instructive: codes may support accuracy in the short term but appear insufficient to sustain it.

Notably, learners reported significantly lower cognitive load when revising after direct corrections on grammatical errors than after metalinguistic codes on grammatical and non-grammatical errors (Bonilla López et al., 2018).
The authors acknowledge they could not employ an online physiological measure of cognitive load, so this self-report finding warrants caution (Bonilla López et al., 2018).
Evidence on how learners act on codes is thinner and largely indirect.

Liu and Wu (2019) found that students favoured direct correction with metalinguistic explanations (215/447, 48.10%), followed by direct correction alone (111/447, 24.83%), suggesting codes are valued when paired with explanation rather than offered in isolation.
Their descriptive, non-randomised questionnaire design limits inference, and the authors themselves note the data are necessarily descriptive (Liu and Wu, 2019).

Zhang and Hyland (2018) observed a very limited range of revision operations in a second draft, with only seven of 35 errors corrected properly, and reported that automated feedback tended to highlight rather than correct errors.
Across the library, metalinguistic codes appear effective for immediate accuracy but weaker than direct correction for retention, and their uptake depends on how learners interpret and value them.

However, only one experimental study isolates codes as a condition (Bonilla López et al., 2018), and no study in the library examines coded feedback alongside peer and automated conditions within a single design.
This gap motivates the present demonstration.

quotes: Low intermediate EFL writers (N = 139) were randomly assigned to four experimental conditions (direct corrections on grammatical errors, metalinguistic codes on grammatical errors, direct corrections on grammatical and non-grammatical errors, or metalinguistic codes on grammatical and non-grammatical errors) and a control group (self-correction).

The participants were randomly assigned to five groups: direct CF on grammatical errors (n = 29), metalinguistic CF with codes on grammatical errors (n = 28), direct CF on grammatical and non-grammatical errors (n = 27), metalinguistic CF with codes on grammatical and non-grammatical errors (n = 28), and a control group (n = 27).
The study also had a self-correction (i.e., control) group (hereafter SC), where learners did not receive any corrections in their text.
Their native language was Spanish, and their mean English proficiency level was lower intermediate (SD = .79) as ascertained by Oxfords’ Quick Placement test (QPT)

verifications.claim_text: Experimental evidence on accuracy comes from Bonilla López et al. (2018), who randomly assigned low-intermediate EFL writers (N = 139) to four feedback conditions and a self-correction control.
verifications.explanation: The source states that "Low intermediate EFL writers (N = 139) were randomly assigned to four experimental conditions (direct corrections on grammatical errors, metalinguistic codes on grammatical errors, direct corrections on grammatical and non-grammatical errors, or metalinguistic codes on grammatical and non-grammatical errors) and a control group (self-correction)." This supports every proposition of the claim: the population (low-intermediate EFL writers, N = 139), the random assignment, the four feedback conditions, and the self-correction control group. The paper also reports accuracy outcomes (immediate and long-term grammatical and non-grammatical accuracy), so the "experimental evidence on accuracy" framing is supported. The only element not directly stated in the chunks is the publication year 2018, which is a bibliographic detail of the citing context rather than a substantive proposition about the study; the study is self-referentially described throughout as the present study by Bonilla López et al.

verifications.claim_text: learners reported significantly lower cognitive load when revising after direct corrections on grammatical errors than after metalinguistic codes on grammatical and non-grammatical errors
verifications.explanation: The central assertion — that reported cognitive load after revision following direct corrections on grammatical errors (DCF+G) was significantly lower than after metalinguistic codes on grammatical and non-grammatical errors (ME+GN) — is stated directly in section 5.4: "the cognitive load imposed by revision after DCF+G was significantly lower than that after ME+GN (p < 0.001, SE = 0.350)", and corroborated in Table 3 ("***ME+GN > DCF+G 1.91 [0.95, 2.88]") and the abstract ("learners’ cognitive load estimates proved significantly lower processing direct corrections targeting grammatical issues"). The peripheral assertions (population = learners in the study; measure = self-reported mental effort/cognitive load after text revision) are also supported by the mental-effort scale description and the significant condition effect on reported mental effort. uncited_sentences.sentence: Metalinguistic coded feedback—error codes with brief explanatory labels that flag an error without supplying the correct form—has been examined as a distinct written corrective feedback (WCF) condition in this literature.

The evidence base in the project library is small and uneven, with the strongest experimental comparison and the main preference data coming from different designs, so conclusions about codes relative to other feedback types remain tentative.
The design is rigorous in its random assignment and delayed posttest, but the self-report measure limits what can be claimed about processing effort.
Learner preferences point in a different direction.
Preference data of this kind indicate valuation, not effect on accuracy or revision.
Evidence on revision behaviour is indirect.
The study was a naturalistic case study of two Chinese students over a 16-week semester, so it cannot speak directly to coded feedback.
Taken together, the library suggests codes may support immediate accuracy but appear weaker than direct correction for retention, with uptake likely shaped by learner preference.
No study in the library compares coded feedback with peer and automated conditions within a single design, which is the gap the present study addresses.
